The Redmouth grouper (Aethaloperca rogaa) is a medium-sized epinephelid that inhabits coral reef slopes and lagoons across the Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from pelagic eggs after approximately 5 days at a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], with the age at birth recorded as 5 days [ab = 5 days]. This brief embryonic phase is characteristic of many serranids that spawn in warm tropical waters. The wet weight at birth is an extraordinarily low 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], reflecting the small diameter of the fertilised ovum, which measures roughly 0.76 mm. Such a minute initial mass imposes a tight energetic constraint on the yolk-dependent prolarva, which must rapidly develop feeding structures before the endogenous yolk reserves are exhausted. Shortly after the exotrophic transition, the free-swimming larva enters a planktonic phase that may last several weeks before settlement onto suitable reef substrates.


Adult Redmouth grouper attain an ultimate total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], placing them among the moderately sized members of the family Epinephelidae. This asymptotic length is reached after a prolonged growth period that spans several years in tropical environments. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this size is approximately 3557 grams [Wwi = approximately 3557 grams], a value derived from length–weight relationships typical of large-bodied coral reef groupers. Comparatively, congeneric species such as Aethaloperca rogaa exhibit a somewhat robust body form, which is reflected in the substantial mass achieved at maximum size. The growth trajectory from the minute 0.00023 gram hatchling to the fully grown adult represents an increase of more than 15 million times in biomass, underscoring the remarkable capacity for somatic expansion in this lineage. These size attributes have implications for the species' trophic ecology, as larger individuals can exploit a broader range of prey.

Sexual maturity in Aethaloperca rogaa is attained at a total length of approximately 34 centimeters [Lp = approximately 34 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 625 grams [Wwp = 625 grams]. This size threshold typically is reached after several years of growth in the wild. The onset of reproductive activity is marked by the activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis, leading to gametogenesis and the first spawning event. Field observations indicate that the age at first reproduction coincides with the attainment of this critical body size, which ensures that females have accrued sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic demands of vitellogenesis and spawning. The relatively large size at maturity, compared to the small birth mass, reflects the extended juvenile phase characteristic of many long-lived, slow-maturing coral reef fishes.

The maximum reproductive output of the Redmouth grouper is substantial, reflecting its position as a high-fecundity batch spawner within the Epinephelidae. Under optimal conditions at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], females produce approximately 1,891,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,891,000 eggs per spawning event], and they may spawn once per year [F_R_i = once per year]. This very high fecundity per event compensates for potential low larval survival rates in the planktonic environment. The spawning season is typically protracted, lasting several months during the warmer period, and is synchronized with lunar cycles to maximize the dispersal and survival of the pelagic larvae. The estimated daily reproduction rate derived from these values is approximately 1,891,000 eggs per year, which is among the highest recorded for serranids of comparable body size.

Longevity records for Aethaloperca rogaa indicate a maximum lifespan of 31 years [am = 31 years] at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], placing it among the longer-lived serranids. This extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by slow growth, late maturity, and high fecundity — a combination typical of many large coral reef groupers. The oldest documented individuals have been collected from protected reef systems where fishing pressure is minimal. Comparative studies within the family Epinephelidae suggest that longevity is positively correlated with asymptotic body size, a pattern that holds well for this species. The combination of a long maximum lifespan (31 years) with a relatively late age at first reproduction and exceptionally high fecundity per event positions Aethaloperca rogaa as a representative of the conservative, K-selected reproductive strategy common among large, slow-growing marine teleosts.
